sections.h: Wisdom of Solomon: Wisdom beside God's throne
sections.b: Chapters 6 to 10 of the Wisdom of Solomon hold the fullest picture of Wisdom as a person outside Proverbs. She goes looking for those worthy of her and waits at their gates (6:12–16). She is the one "who crafted all things" (7:22), with a spirit of twenty-one marks, "a vapor rising from God's power, / a clean outflow of the Almighty's glory" and "a radiance of eternal light" (7:25–26). She lives with God, shares his knowledge and sits beside his thrones (8:3–4; 9:4). The king courts her as a bride (8:2) and prays, "Give me Wisdom" (9:4). Then chapter 10 shows her saving the righteous from Adam to Moses. Much of this language was later used of Christ (Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 6:12–16; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–8:1; Wisdom of Solomon 9:4; Wisdom of Solomon 10:1–21; Proverbs 8:22–31; Hebrews 1:3

common: Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 calls Wisdom apaugasma, 'radiance', the word Hebrews 1:3 uses of the Son.
uncommon: The Wisdom of Solomon may have been written partly to offer Jewish wisdom to Greek rulers and thinkers, not only to Jews.

sections.h: Solomon's voice in the Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 7 to 9 is spoken by a king who prayed for wisdom, was told to build the temple and calls David his father, though the book never names him. He is a mortal born like everyone (7:1–6), who chose wisdom over thrones (7:8), learned all the sciences (7:17–21), courted Wisdom as a bride (8:2) and prayed for her (9:1–18), recalling 1 Kings 3:5–14 and the command to build the temple (9:7–8). The book's front page sets out who wrote it.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:1–9:18; 1 Kings 3:5–14; 1 Kings 4:29–34; 2 Chronicles 1:7–12

sections.h: A good soul and an undefiled body (Wisdom 8:19–20)
sections.b: The speaker says, "a good soul was given me as my share. Or better, since I was good, I came into a body without stain" (8:19–20). The verse can be read as the soul existing before the body, as in Plato, or as naming the soul as the true self. Origen taught that souls existed before bodies (On First Principles 2.9.6). The fifteen anathemas against Origen usually assigned to the Second Council of Constantinople (553) begin by condemning "the fabulous pre-existence of souls"; whether that council adopted them, or a synod at Constantinople in 543, is disputed. Later teachers asked instead where each soul comes from: the Catholic Catechism says each is "created immediately by God" (366), the Lutheran Quenstedt taught that souls are passed on from the parents, and Latter-day Saints teach a life before birth. The book also says that "a perishable body is a weight on the soul" (9:15), a line Augustine quoted many times. See the card at Wisdom 8.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 8:19–20; Wisdom of Solomon 9:15; Wisdom of Solomon 6:18–19; Wisdom of Solomon 8:13; Wisdom of Solomon 8:17

sections.b: Wisdom is "a radiance of eternal light, / a stainless mirror of God's working, / an image of his goodness" (7:26). Hebrews uses the same word for the Son, "the brightness that shines out from God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3), and Colossians calls him "the image of the God who cannot be seen" (Colossians 1:15). Origen explained 7:25–26 of the Son (On First Principles 1.2.9), and in the Arian controversy Athanasius argued from the radiance image that the Son never was not, since light is never without its radiance (Orations against the Arians 1.13).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–26; Hebrews 1:3; Colossians 1:15; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 1:24

sections.b: Solomon's prayer asks, "Who has known your plan, unless you gave wisdom / and sent your Holy Spirit down from the heights?" (9:17). Wisdom and God's Holy Spirit are named side by side as one gift; Wisdom herself has "a spirit that thinks, that is holy" (7:22), and a "spirit of wisdom" came to the king when he prayed (7:7). Paul makes the same point: only God's Spirit knows God's mind (1 Corinthians 2:10–12).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:7; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22; Wisdom of Solomon 9:17; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12; Isaiah 11:2

sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon 6 tells kings that "your power was given to you by the Lord" (6:3), that they are "servants of his kingdom" (6:4), and that "the powerful will be powerfully examined" (6:6). A wise king "keeps a people steady" (6:24), and longing for wisdom "lifts a person to a kingdom" (6:20).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 6:1–11; Wisdom of Solomon 6:20–24; Proverbs 8:15–16; Romans 13:1–4

sections.b: Solomon says of Wisdom, "I wanted to bring her home as my bride, / and I fell in love with her beauty" (8:2). He decides to bring her home to share his life (8:9), and "living with her" has no pain (8:16). Wisdom herself shares her life with God (8:3). Proverbs had already urged young men to love Wisdom like a wife (Proverbs 4:6–8; 7:4).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 8:2–18; Proverbs 4:6–8; Proverbs 7:4; Proverbs 31:10

sections.h: A copy of the heavenly tent (Wisdom 9:8)
sections.b: Solomon's prayer calls the temple and its altar a copy, "modeled on the holy tent you made ready at the beginning" (9:8). The idea that the earthly sanctuary copies a heavenly one goes back to the pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40) and is the basis of Hebrews 8:5 and 9:24.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 9:8; Exodus 25:9; Exodus 25:40; Hebrews 8:5; Hebrews 9:24

sections.b: Before Hebrews 11 listed the heroes of faith, Wisdom of Solomon 10 listed seven righteous people saved by Wisdom: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph and Moses with Israel, each set against a wicked counterpart (Cain, Babel, the Five Cities, Esau, Joseph's accusers, Egypt). No one is named. The thread is wisdom where Hebrews has faith.

sections.h: Cain in the Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom 10:3–4 calls Cain "an unrighteous man" who left Wisdom in his anger and "was destroyed together with the fury in which he killed his brother," and says the Flood came "because of him." Genesis says Cain lived on and built a city (Genesis 4:15–17), so "destroyed" may mean ruin of the soul.

Wisdom of Solomon says that when Jacob fled from Esau, Wisdom "let him see God's kingdom / and taught him about holy things" (10:10), its reading of the stairway and the angels at Bethel (Genesis 28:12).

sections.h: The crossing in the Wisdom of Solomon
sections.b: Wisdom 10:18–20 says Wisdom took Israel "across the Red Sea" (the Greek name), drowned their enemies, and "threw them up out of the depths of the abyss," so that the righteous took their spoils. Josephus tells a related story: the Egyptians' weapons washed up at the Hebrews' camp (Jewish Antiquities 2.349).

Among the sciences God taught the wise king are "the many kinds of plants and the powers in roots" (7:20), the herbal medicine of the ancient world, counted as a gift of God. The book also counts ten months in the womb (7:2).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:2; Wisdom of Solomon 7:17–20; Sirach 38:1–8; 1 Kings 4:33

sections.h: Knowledge of the stars as God's gift (Wisdom 7:18–19)
sections.b: Solomon says God taught him the solstices, the seasons, "the circling of the years, the positions of the stars" (7:18–19): knowledge for the calendar, not fortune-telling. Later the book rebukes those who took the stars for gods (13:2).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 7:17–19; Wisdom of Solomon 13:2; Genesis 1:14

sections.h: The four virtues claimed for Wisdom (Wisdom 8:7)
sections.b: Wisdom of Solomon says Wisdom "teaches self-control and understanding, / righteousness and courage" (8:7), the four chief virtues of Greek philosophy since Plato, later called the cardinal virtues. A Jew in a Greek city is told that the best of Greek ethics belongs to the Wisdom of Israel's God. The same chapters use the language of mystery cults (6:22; 8:4) and Stoic philosophy (7:22–24).
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 8:7; Wisdom of Solomon 6:22; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22–24; Wisdom of Solomon 8:4

sections.b: Solomon knew he would not win Wisdom "any other way, unless God gave her," and that knowing whose gift she is "was itself a sign of understanding" (8:21). The Latin read the verse as "I could not be continent unless God gave it," and Augustine quoted it in his Confessions (6.11.20; 10.31.45): even self-control is God's gift.
sections.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 8:21; James 1:5; James 1:17; 1 Corinthians 4:7
